title: Raft: electing a new leader

steps.say: S1 is the leader of term 1. Every 50 ms it sends an empty AppendEntries as a heartbeat, so followers know it is alive.
S1 crashes and the heartbeats stop. S2 and S3 each wait for a random election timeout between 150 and 300 ms.
S3's timer (170 ms) fires first. It becomes a candidate, adds 1 to the term (now 2) and votes for itself.
S3 asks everyone for a vote. The message to S1 is lost because S1 is down.
S2 has not voted in term 2 and S3's log is at least as new as its own, so it says yes. S3 now has 2 of 3 votes: a majority.
S3 becomes leader of term 2 and sends heartbeats at once, so nobody else starts an election.
S1 restarts. It still believes it is leader of term 1 and sends an old AppendEntries.
S2 rejects it, because term 2 is higher than 1. S1 sees the higher term and steps down to follower. A deposed leader cannot do harm.
Failure case: if S1 and S2 both time out together, each votes for itself. Neither gets 2 votes, so the term ends with no leader. They retry in term 3 with new random timeouts.

title: Raft: copying a log entry

steps.say: S3 is behind: it holds only 4 entries because it was offline for a while. The leader S1 and S2 have 6.
A client sends the command x=5 to the leader. The leader appends it as entry 7 (term 2) to its own log. It is not committed yet.
The leader sends AppendEntries (prev=6, entry 7) to both followers. The copy to S3 is lost on the network.
S2 checks that its entry 6 matches, stores entry 7 and answers OK. The leader now has 2 of 3 copies, which is a majority.
Entry 7 is committed. The leader applies x=5 and replies to the client. Even if S1 dies now, entry 7 survives on S2.
At the next heartbeat the leader tries S3 again. S3 has no entry 6, so the check on prev=6 fails and it rejects the message.
The leader lowers its nextIndex for S3 from 7 to 5 and sends entries 5, 6 and 7 together.
S3 matches at entry 4, stores 5 to 7 and says OK. All three logs are now identical.

title: Paxos: choosing one value

steps.say: Three acceptors vote on one value. Proposer 1 wants X. A proposal needs a number so newer ones win: it picks n=5.
Phase 1: Proposer 1 sends Prepare(n=5). Each acceptor promises to ignore any proposal with a number below 5.
All three promise. None has accepted anything yet, so Proposer 1 is free to use X.
Phase 2: Proposer 1 sends Accept(5, X). The message to Acceptor 3 is lost.
Acceptors 1 and 2 accept (5, X). Two of three is a majority, so X is now chosen forever, even though Acceptor 3 never heard.
Failure case: Proposer 2 never heard the news and wants Y. It sends Prepare(n=6) to Acceptors 2 and 3.
Acceptor 2 replies with what it already accepted: (5, X). Acceptor 3 has nothing. Any majority must overlap with the first one, so Proposer 2 will always see X.
The rule: if any promise carries an accepted value, the proposer must use it. Proposer 2 drops Y and sends Accept(6, X).
All three now hold X (Acceptor 3 joins in). The chosen value never changed, which is the safety guarantee of Paxos.

title: Two-phase commit and its blocking

steps.say: A purchase must change three databases, all or none. The coordinator starts a transaction and asks everyone if they are ready.
Phase 1 (prepare): the coordinator sends Prepare to all three.
Each database writes the change to its log, takes locks and votes yes. A database that voted yes may not change its mind.
The coordinator writes COMMIT to its own log first. This is the moment the decision becomes final.
Phase 2: Commit goes to all three. They apply the change, release locks and acknowledge. Total cost: 2 round trips and 3 log writes per database.
Failure case, next purchase: all three vote yes and sit prepared with locks held.
The coordinator crashes before sending any decision. The databases cannot commit (someone may have voted no) and cannot abort (the coordinator may have chosen commit).
They are blocked. Their locks stay held, so other orders on those rows wait. After 30 s of waiting nothing has changed.
When the coordinator restarts it reads its log, finds no decision, and aborts. It resends Abort and the locks are finally released.

title: Quorums: N=3, W=2, R=2

steps.say: Three replicas hold x=1 (version 1). We choose W=2 (writes must reach 2 replicas) and R=2 (reads ask 2). Since 2+2 is more than 3, any write set and read set must share a replica.
The client writes x=2. It sends the write to all three replicas. The copy to Replica 3 is lost.
Replicas 1 and 2 store it and acknowledge. That is W=2, so the write succeeds although Replica 3 is stale.
A read asks Replicas 2 and 3. They answer v2 and v1 (the old one).
The client keeps the highest version, v2. The overlap on Replica 2 guarantees the read sees the latest write. Result: x=2.
Failure case: now use W=1 and R=1, for speed. A write x=3 reaches only Replica 1 and succeeds.
A read from Replica 3 returns x=1 (v1). No overlap, so the client gets stale data and cannot even tell.
Trade-off: bigger W and R are safer but slower, and fail if too many replicas are down. With N=3, W=2, R=2 you can lose one replica and keep working.

title: Async replication loses an acknowledged write

steps.say: One leader takes all writes and copies them to two followers. Here the copy is asynchronous: the leader does not wait for it.
The client writes x=2. The leader saves it and answers 'done' at once, in about 1 ms.
In the background the leader ships x=2 to both followers. They apply it a few milliseconds later (replication lag).
The client writes x=3. Again the leader answers 'done' immediately, before any follower has the new value.
Failure case: the leader crashes 5 ms later, before it sent x=3. The copies in flight are lost.
Follower 1 is promoted to leader. It holds x=2. The write x=3, which the client was told succeeded, is gone for good.
Fix: synchronous replication. The client writes x=4 and the leader first waits for at least one follower to confirm.
Only now does the leader reply 'done'. A crash can no longer lose this write. The cost: each write is slower, and if the follower is down, writes stall.

title: Kafka ISR shrinks and min.insync.replicas

steps.say: A partition has 3 copies. The ISR is the list of copies that are fully caught up. The producer uses acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2.
The producer sends a message. The leader writes it at offset 41 and the two followers copy it.
Both followers confirm. The high watermark moves to 41 and the producer gets its ack. Consumers can now read offset 41.
Broker 3 has a slow disk and falls to offset 38. After 30 s behind (replica.lag.time.max.ms) the leader removes it from the ISR.
A message at offset 42 now needs acks only from the ISR, which is Brokers 1 and 2. It succeeds. The slow broker no longer holds back writers.
Failure case: Broker 2 crashes. The ISR is just {1}, smaller than min.insync=2.
The leader refuses new writes and returns NotEnoughReplicas. The producer sees an error instead of a write held by one broker only.
Worse: Broker 1 dies too. Only Broker 3 is alive and it is missing offsets 39 to 42. Nobody in the ISR is left.
Default (unclean election off): the partition stays offline until Broker 1 or 2 returns. If you turn it on, Broker 3 leads and 4 acknowledged messages are lost.

title: A leader lease and a paused leader

steps.say: Only one node may act as leader. The rule: a node is leader only while it holds a lease, a lock with a time limit (TTL).
Node A asks for the lease with a TTL of 10 s. The store is free, so it grants it. A becomes leader.
A renews every 3 s, resetting the TTL to 10 s. Normal life: A writes to the disk and B waits.
Failure case: A freezes for 15 s in a long garbage-collection pause. It sends no renewals and does not know time is passing.
After 10 s with no renewal the lease expires. The store frees it.
Node B asks for the lease and gets it. B is now the leader, and that is the right call because A looked dead.
A wakes up at second 15. Its last check said 'I am leader', so it writes. Now two leaders write at once: split brain.
A's next renew fails because the store says B owns the lease. A steps down, but its stale write already got through.

Lesson: a lease alone is not safe, since a pause can hit right after the check. The disk must also reject old leaders, with fencing tokens. Keep TTL short enough for fast failover (10 s) but long enough to survive small hiccups.

title: Consistent hashing: adding and losing a node

steps.say: Servers A, B, C sit on a ring at positions 0, 120 and 240. The hash of a key picks a position, and the key belongs to the first server clockwise from it.
Key k1 hashes to 60, k2 to 180 and k3 to 300. Walking clockwise, k1 goes to B (120), k2 to C (240) and k3 to A (360, which is 0).
Add server D at position 210. It takes over only the arc between B (120) and D (210).
Only k2 (at 180) lies in that arc, so only k2 moves from C to D. k1 and k3 stay. With N servers, about 1/N of keys move; a plain 'hash mod N' would move almost all.
Failure case: server B crashes.
B's keys slide clockwise to the next server. k1 (60) now lands on D at 210. Everyone else is untouched.
Problem: D now holds a big arc and may get 2x the load. Real systems give each server many positions (for example 256 virtual nodes), so a crashed server's load spreads over all others.

title: Gossip spreads an update

steps.say: Six nodes all hold x=1. There is no leader. Every second, each node that knows news picks 2 random peers and tells them.
Node 1 gets a write: x=9. At second 0, only Node 1 knows it.
Round 1: Node 1 tells Nodes 3 and 4. Now 3 of 6 know. The number of informed nodes roughly doubles every round.
Failure case: Node 6 is down. Round 2: Node 1 tries Node 6 and the message is lost, but Nodes 3 and 4 reach Nodes 2 and 5.
Five nodes know x=9 after 2 rounds. No single lost message mattered, since many other paths exist.
Round 3: nodes also pick peers who already know. Those say 'have it' and nothing changes. This waste is the price of having no coordinator.
Node 6 comes back still holding x=1.
Round 4: Node 2 picks Node 6 by chance and tells it. All six agree. With 1000 nodes this still takes only about 10 to 15 rounds, because growth is exponential.

title: Vector clocks find concurrent writes

steps.say: Each replica stores a cart and a vector clock: one counter for each replica, written [A,B,C]. All start at [0,0,0].
A client adds milk through Replica A. A bumps its own slot: cart [milk] with clock [1,0,0].
A copies the version to B. B now holds the same cart and clock [1,0,0]. Same clock means same version.
Failure case: the link between A and B breaks. A client adds eggs through B. B bumps its slot: clock [1,1,0].
At the same time another client adds bread through A, which bumps its slot: clock [2,0,0]. Neither replica knows about the other write.
The link heals and A sends its version to B. B compares [2,0,0] with its own [1,1,0].
Rule: one clock wins if every slot is greater or equal. Here 2>1 in slot A but 0<1 in slot B, so neither wins. The writes were concurrent: a conflict.
B keeps both versions and shows both to the next reader. The client merges them to [milk,eggs,bread] and writes back with clock [3,1,0], which beats both.

title: Lamport clocks: ordering without a shared clock

actors.label: Rule
actors.sub: send: clock+1, attach it. receive: max(own, received)+1

steps.say: Three machines have clocks that disagree, so we use counters instead. Rule: add 1 for every event; on receiving a message, jump to max(own, received) + 1.
P1 does a local event. Its clock goes from 0 to 1.
P1 sends m1 to P2. Sending is an event: P1 goes to 2 and stamps the message with 2.
P2 had clock 0. It receives ts=2 and sets clock = max(0,2)+1 = 3. Now the receive is stamped later than the send.
P2 sends m2 to P3 with ts=4. The message is lost. P3 still shows 0 and does not know anything happened.
P2 sends again as a new event: ts=5. P3 gets it and sets clock = max(0,5)+1 = 6. The jump keeps P3 consistent without any resend logic.
Meanwhile P1 does another local event: clock 3. P1's event (3) and P2's receive (3) have the same number but are unrelated.

nt.label: Rule
nt.sub: equal numbers: break tie by node id

steps.say: Limit: if event a caused event b, then clock(a) < clock(b). The reverse is false. P1's event (3) is below P3's (6) yet did not cause it. Lamport clocks cannot show 'concurrent'; vector clocks can.

nt.label: Rule
nt.sub: smaller number does not mean caused

title: A CRDT counter merges after a partition

actors.label: Merge rule
actors.sub: per slot: take the larger number

steps.say: A 'like' counter is kept on two replicas. Each replica has one slot per replica and only changes its own slot. The value is the sum of all slots.
Failure case: the network between them is cut. Both replicas keep accepting likes, with no coordination.
Two users like on Replica 1. It bumps its own slot: {R1:2, R2:0}, value 2.
One user likes on Replica 2: {R1:0, R2:1}, value 1. The replicas disagree but nothing has been lost.
The network heals. Each replica sends its full state to the other.
Each takes the larger number per slot: max(2,0)=2 and max(0,1)=1. Both now hold {R1:2, R2:1} and show 3 likes, the true total.
The network delivers the same message twice. Taking the max again changes nothing: still 3. A plain '+=' counter would now say 5.
Why it works: merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so order, delays and duplicates do not matter. Limit: this counter only grows. Likes and unlikes need two such counters (a PN-counter).

nt.label: Merge rule
nt.sub: any order, any repeats: same result

title: Read repair and anti-entropy

steps.say: Three replicas store each key with a timestamp. Replica 3 was down during the last update, so it still has the old name=Bob @90. Replicas 1 and 2 have name=Ann @105.
A client reads 'name'. The coordinator asks all three replicas.
The answers differ: Ann @105, Ann @105 and Bob @90. The coordinator picks the newest timestamp and returns Ann.
Read repair: before finishing, the coordinator writes the newest value back to the stale replica. Replica 3 is fixed for free during a normal read.
Failure case: read repair only fixes keys that get read. Key 'z' has not been read for months. Replica 2 missed its update: it has z=1 @40, others z=2 @50.
Anti-entropy runs in the background. Every 10 minutes Replicas 1 and 2 compare the roots of their Merkle trees (hash trees over key ranges). The roots differ.
They compare child hashes level by level and find the one key range that differs. This takes about 20 small comparisons, not a scan of millions of keys.
Only that range is sent. Replica 2 takes z=2 @50 because 50 is newer than 40. All replicas now agree without anyone reading the key.
Deleted keys are kept as tombstones for a while (for example 10 days). Without them, a replica that missed the delete would send the old value back and the key would come alive again.

title: Merkle trees find the one different block

steps.say: Two replicas each hold 4 data blocks. A leaf is the hash of one block, a parent is the hash of its two children, and the root summarizes everything. Both roots are c3, so one comparison proves all 4 blocks match.
Replica B missed an update, so block 3 differs. Its leaf hash changes to 5d, and the change climbs: h34 becomes d8 and the root becomes 8e.
Step 1: compare the roots. c3 and 8e are different, so something is out of sync. One small message, not the data.
Step 2: compare the two children. h12 matches, so blocks 1 and 2 are skipped without being looked at. h34 differs.
Step 3: compare the leaves under h34. h4 matches, h3 differs. We found the single bad block in 3 steps.
Only block 3 is copied from A to B. For 1 million blocks the same search needs about 20 levels, not 1 million comparisons.
B recomputes its hashes up the path: h3 e0, h34 27, root c3. The roots are equal again. The same check detects tampering, since changing any byte changes the root.

title: A fencing token stops a paused client

steps.say: The lock service gives each new lock holder a number that always goes up. This number is the fencing token. Storage will check it.
Client A asks for the lock and gets it with token 33. The lease lasts 10 s.
A writes to storage and sends its token. Storage accepts and remembers the highest token seen: 33.
Failure case: A freezes for 20 s in a garbage-collection pause. It does not know its lease is running out.
After 10 s the lease expires. Client B asks for the lock and gets token 34.
B writes with token 34. Storage accepts it and now remembers 34.
A wakes up after 20 s and still believes it holds the lock. It sends its write with token 33.
Storage sees 33 is lower than 34 and rejects the write. B's data is safe. Without this check, A's stale write would overwrite B's.
Lesson: the lock service cannot stop a paused client, because the client cannot know it is paused. The resource itself must check tokens.

title: Why a replay doubles the balance

steps.say: A consumer reads messages from a log and updates a database. It saves its position (the committed offset) after the work. Offset 99 is committed. Next is offset 100: 'add 50'.
The consumer reads offset 100.
It writes to the database. The balance goes from 0 to 50. This is correct so far.
Failure case: the consumer crashes before it commits offset 100. The database change is saved, but the log does not know.
The consumer restarts and asks where it was. The answer is 99, so it reads offset 100 again. This is at-least-once delivery.
It adds 50 again. The balance is 100 but should be 50. The customer was charged twice.
Fix: store the offset in the same database transaction as the result. Next message, offset 101 'add 20': one transaction sets the balance to 70 and the offset to 101, all or nothing.
The consumer crashes again before committing to the log. Because the DB holds the position, the log's commit no longer matters.

On restart the consumer reads offset 101 again, but first asks the DB: 'last offset?' The answer is 101, so it skips the message. Balance stays 70. The effect is exactly once, though delivery was twice.

title: The outbox pattern

steps.say: When an order is saved, other services must hear about it. The naive way: save to the database, then publish to the broker. That is two writes to two systems, and no transaction covers both.
The service saves order 17 to the database.
Failure case: the service crashes right now, before it publishes. The order exists but 'order created' was never sent. Billing and shipping never find out, and nothing will fix it.
Fix: the service writes the order row and an outbox row (event e17) in ONE database transaction. Either both exist or neither does.
A relay process polls the outbox table every 500 ms and finds the unsent row e17.
The relay publishes e17 to the broker. The consumer processes it.
Failure case: the relay crashes before it marks e17 as sent. The row is still marked unsent.
After restart the relay polls again, sees e17 unsent, and publishes it a second time. Delivery is at-least-once: duplicates can happen, but loss cannot.
The consumer remembers event ids it has handled, sees e17 again and ignores it. Outbox plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once.

title: A saga undoes steps with compensations

steps.say: An order needs payment, then a stock reservation, in different services with different databases. A saga runs them one after another, each as its own local transaction.
Step 1: the order service asks Payment to charge 40 USD. Payment commits locally and confirms.
Step 2: it asks Stock to reserve the item. Failure case: the stock is 0, so Stock refuses.
There is no global rollback; the 40 USD is already charged. Instead the saga runs a compensation: a new action that undoes the effect. Here it is a refund.
Failure case: the refund request gets lost, so Payment never sees it. The order service waits for a reply, with a 5 s timeout.
After the timeout the order service sends the refund again with the same request id r9.
Payment refunds once and replies. If the retry arrived twice, the id r9 lets Payment ignore the second one.
The saga ends in a clean state: order 17 is cancelled. Compensations must be safe to repeat, and the saga's progress must be saved, so a crash can resume it.

title: Heartbeats and a timeout

steps.say: Every node sends a heartbeat to the monitor once per second. The monitor marks a node dead if it hears nothing for 3 s.
One heartbeat from Node 2 is lost in the network. The monitor waits; the gap is only 2 s, below 3 s. Next second Node 2 beats again. One loss is not a failure.
Node 3 crashes. Its beats stop.
1 s and then 2 s pass with nothing from Node 3. The monitor is suspicious but waits.
At 3 s the timeout fires. The monitor declares Node 3 dead and the cluster starts failover. Detection time is about 3 s.
False alarm: Node 2 freezes for 4 s in a garbage-collection pause. It is not dead, only silent, but the monitor cannot tell the difference.
The monitor declares Node 2 dead too. Its work is moved to others, which wastes effort and can cause a split brain.
Node 2 wakes and sends a beat. The monitor marks it alive again.

Trade-off: a 3 s timeout is fast but gives false alarms; 30 s gives fewer false alarms but a slower reaction. Better detectors (phi accrual) learn the usual gap between beats and score how unlikely the silence is.

title: A circuit breaker opens, then probes

steps.say: The client calls the service through a breaker. Every call has a timeout of 500 ms. While the breaker is closed, calls go straight through.
The service gets sick and takes 5 s per call. The client gives up after 500 ms each time. Each timeout counts as a failure; meanwhile client threads sit waiting.
The rule: 5 failures within 10 s. The 5th failure arrives and the breaker trips to open.
While open, calls fail in under 1 ms and never reach the service. The client frees its threads and can use a fallback. The sick service gets quiet time to recover.
After 30 s the breaker goes half-open and lets exactly one probe call through. The service is still sick, so the probe times out.
The probe failed, so the breaker opens again for another 30 s. A flood of full traffic never hit the sick service.
30 s later, the second probe goes through. The service is healthy now and answers in 20 ms.
The breaker closes and normal traffic resumes. Without it, thousands of calls waiting 5 s each would have used up all the client's threads and spread the failure upstream.

title: Retry storm and backoff with jitter

steps.say: 1000 clients call a server. Normal load is 100 requests per second; the server can handle 150.
The server stalls for 1 s (a short hiccup). Requests time out.
Naive retry: every client retries exactly 1 s later. All 1000 failed requests arrive in the same instant, on top of normal traffic: about 1100 per second, 7 times the limit.
The server drowns and times out again. Everyone retries again at 2 s, and again at 3 s. This is a retry storm: the retries keep the server down after the original problem is gone.
Fix part 1, exponential backoff: wait longer after each failure. Waits of 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, doubling up to a cap of 30 s.
Fix part 2, jitter: pick a random wait between 0 and the backoff, so clients do not move together. Client 1 draws 0.3 s and retries first, successfully.
Client 2 drew 0.7 s. Client 3 drew 0.9 s. They arrive one by one instead of all at once.
The 1000 retries are now spread over about a second, so the load peaks near 120 per second, under the limit of 150.
Also set a retry budget: at most 3 attempts per request, and retry only safe (idempotent) calls. Together with a circuit breaker, retries help the server recover instead of hurting it.
